A generation from preparation to engine launch

html:
Portal planning, generations and worker cleanup

The shared Portal turns a requested model profile into a supervised serving generation. It owns planning, model preparation, resource leases, process launch, readiness and cleanup. The Controller adds the task-admission and receipt ordering described in Controller inference lifecycle. Standalone hosts expose the same worker operations through their own API.

The main owners are Portal, Supervisor, placement planning, parallelism policy, command construction and Portal storage. Use the shared architecture overview for installation, storage and diagnostic ownership, and the Inference manual for operator workflows.

Requested, resolved and running state

flowchart TD U[Saved profile or explicit launch request] --> R[Requested snapshot] H[Host and model inventory] --> P[Planner and runtime policies] C[Inspected runtime capabilities] --> P R --> P P --> V[Preview with errors and estimates] P --> E[Resolved generation snapshot] E --> A[Arguments and environment] A --> W[Generation-owned workers] W --> O[Health, placement and configuration evidence] O --> S[Published ready generation] S --> B[Successful requested and resolved snapshots] B --> N[Recovery or explicit restoration]

Saving a profile does not change an existing engine. A normal start validates a copy of the request, records desired-running state and schedules one coordinator per instance. Concurrent starts reuse an active coordinator. A pending stop or force-stop must finish before a new start can enter the instance lock.

Requested settings remain separate from the effective launch. Recommendations can select a different GPU subset or split using current observations without editing the saved profile. Tensor mode uses independent settings and resolves an effective copy; saved Pipeline settings remain available. Explicit Tensor mode requires selected GPUs on the serving host. A one-GPU selection resolves to single-device execution, while advertised Tensor support is required for multiple GPUs.

Readiness retains both successful snapshots. The launch-request selector prefers the successful requested snapshot for recovery, falling back to the successful resolved snapshot for older records. Exact rollback supplies the prior resolved profile with recommendation disabled and its original requested snapshot; it validates that layout without resolving it anew or repeating managed fitting.

Planning before resource ownership

sequenceDiagram participant A as Management caller participant P as Portal participant H as Host inventories participant V as Planner and command policies A->>P: Preview requested profile P->>H: Read required hosts, runtimes and serving model H-->>P: Availability and inspected capabilities P->>V: Resolve mode, layout and context V-->>P: Candidate placement, estimates, errors and warnings opt Pipeline model compatibility needs inspection P->>H: Run runtime model-support check H-->>P: Compatibility evidence end P->>V: Compile redacted command and validate cache or fit prerequisites P-->>A: Preview only Note over A,V: No GPU reservation or inference engine launch

Portal.context requires registered online hosts, a ready matching runtime on each required host and a complete model on the serving host. Preview can perform runtime/model compatibility inspection; it is not universally free of subprocess or network activity. It does not load an inference engine or reserve resources.

The planner orders selected devices, validates backend parallelism constraints and computes conservative weight/KV estimates when model metadata permits. Unknown weight or cache semantics stay unknown. Per-device estimated overcommit is a warning, not a measured failure or proof of fit. Distributed vLLM requires compatible runtime stacks and an advertised worker-placement adapter; llama.cpp distribution requires compatible RPC support. The command compiler protects the owners of layout/context flags and validates extra options against the selected runtime.

Finite host-cache RAM is checked against observed memory and managed reservations. GPU/port reservation conflicts are enforced later by each worker supervisor. A preview therefore neither promises resources will still be available nor grants exclusive hardware use. Managed reservations do not exclude unrelated GPU clients. Tensor fitting previews describe a starting candidate; measured trial selection belongs to the launch path.

A generation from preparation to engine launch

sequenceDiagram participant P as Generation coordinator participant H as Required hosts participant S as Host supervisors participant E as Serving engine P->>H: Re-inspect selected runtimes and refresh context P->>P: Validate plan and freeze requested/resolved snapshots P->>H: Prepare model aliases and matching identities loop Each generation member P->>S: Reserve selected GPUs, ports and finite cache RAM S-->>P: Accepted owner/generation lease end P->>P: Start periodic lease renewal alt Distributed vLLM P->>S: Launch owned Ray head, then workers else Distributed llama.cpp P->>S: Launch owned RPC workers and check their ports end P->>P: Resolve secrets and compile final command opt llama.cpp uses selected GPUs P->>H: Discover local/RPC devices and verify order/count end opt Managed Tensor fitting P->>S: Run bounded trials under retained reservations S-->>P: Selected resolved candidate and fit evidence end P->>S: Launch serving engine for this generation S->>E: Spawn owned process and output readers P->>P: Enter loading and begin readiness checks

Each generation has a fresh generation ID and worker job ID. Runtime inspection is repeated before planning so stale UI catalogs do not authorize a changed binary. Model preparation precedes GPU reservation. It can download a missing matching remote model, verify identity and atomically replace a stable alias. Repository source/revision, local GGUF file metadata and local transformer content hashing are different identity paths; a GGUF metadata identity is not a content checksum. Distributed vLLM requires the same absolute model-alias path on every member.

Reservations are acquired member by member with a 90-second lease; successful acknowledgements are retained for cleanup. The coordinator starts renewal every 15 seconds after acquisition. Support workers and the engine share that generation ownership. Secret references are resolved only for executable arguments/environment; presented commands and logs use the redaction owner.

The coordinator checks llama.cpp device discovery against selected local/RPC counts and orders. Distributed vLLM uses Ray placement evidence at readiness. A remote serving host must expose an interface reachable by the coordinator. Port-listener checks for Ray/RPC establish connectivity, not inference readiness.

Worker admission and process ownership

flowchart TD R[Reservation request] --> L[Supervisor admission lock] L --> I[Validate owner, generation and immutable resources] I --> C[Check managed conflicts, RAM and bindable ports] C --> D[Persist lease deadline] D --> W[Worker launch request] W --> F[Require current generation and unexpired lease] F --> A[Resolve command and controlled environment] A --> X{Role already owned?} X -->|Same argv| T[Return existing worker status] X -->|Different argv| N[Reject conflicting role] X -->|New role| V[Recheck runtime identity and engine cache budget] V --> P[Spawn and register child plus readers]

An existing reservation can renew only the same owner, generation, GPU list, ports and RAM budget. New leases check managed GPU/port conflicts, finite cache RAM and temporarily bind each unprivileged port. The bind probe is closed afterward; it is not an OS-level port reservation held until engine startup. The actual process bind can still fail. Worker launch requires a matching live lease and a ready runtime.

Existing-role reuse compares the compiled command; it returns current status rather than applying a new environment or restarting that role. For a new launch, an available runtime fingerprint is compared with fresh identity evidence. Engine cache RAM must equal the reservation and still fit observed available memory. Inherited cache settings cannot silently bypass the profile's budget. Tensor/native fit policies remove conflicting inherited variables through their defined owners.

The supervisor starts a new process session, captures stdout/stderr and retains process handles, role, command, readers and exit tasks. A delegated inference-portal.service cgroup is used when available; arbitrary cgroups are not adopted. An ownership-callback failure stops the child before propagating. Logs feed runtime/configuration observations, build/download progress and generation-scoped rank placement records. Exit observation alone does not release a reservation.

Readiness, health and generation failure

flowchart TD L[Loading generation] --> W[Check renewal task and all member workers] W --> H[Poll engine health within startup deadline] H -->|Not healthy yet| H H --> P[Require expected Ray ranks when distributed] P -->|Awaiting all ranks| H P --> C[Verify serving capabilities and configuration evidence] C --> F[Verify final fit margins when managed fitting] F --> R[Publish ready endpoint and successful snapshots] R --> M[Continue health and bounded metric collection] M -->|Healthy| M M -->|Three unhealthy checks| E[Generation failure] W -->|Lost lease or exited worker| E H -->|Startup timeout| E P -->|Placement mismatch| E C -->|Required validation fails| E F -->|Final fit fails| E E --> O[End observations and request member cleanup]

The readiness deadline is the profile's startup timeout, measured after engine launch. Preparation, support-worker startup and fitting have their own waits. Each health iteration also checks worker presence, return codes and reservations; the health loop notices a failed renewal task. Healthy HTTP alone is insufficient for distributed vLLM: expected rank UUIDs must match the resolved placement.

Serving/template compatibility is verified before readiness. llama.cpp configuration observation can remain unavailable for an ordinary launch; the report records that limit. Managed fitting additionally requires the final observation, memory margins and fitted context to match. A bounded generation probe does not prove full-length context conformance.

After readiness, the loop polls about every three seconds and fails on three consecutive unhealthy observations. Metrics reads have a short timeout and one-MiB bound; only the same ready, observable generation can publish cached values. The timeline consumes those existing metrics.

sequenceDiagram participant C as Instance coordinator participant G as Generation participant S as State store participant H as Prepared hosts loop At most four attempts while desired running C->>G: Launch from original request G->>G: Recompute current plan unless restoring frozen layout G->>H: Prepare and own member workers alt Cancellation G->>G: End observations and cancel renewal G->>H: Request cleanup on acknowledged members G-->>C: Propagate cancellation else Configuration or compatibility ValueError G->>H: Request cleanup for acquired members G-->>C: Configuration failure C->>S: Mark failed without transient retry else Other generation failure G->>H: Request cleanup for acquired members G-->>C: Failure evidence C->>S: Recovering, or failed on fourth attempt C->>C: Wait 2, 4 or 8 seconds before next eligible attempt end end

The generation finalizer invalidates observations, clears metric caches, joins its renewal task and requests cleanup from members whose reservations were acknowledged. Remote cleanup errors are logged as deferred to lease expiry; this is not proof of immediate release. An uncertain remote reservation reply can likewise require the worker's lease-expiry cleanup. Configuration failures end the current coordinator; desired-running intent remains until an explicit lifecycle action changes it. Cancellation propagates and does not become a transient retry.

Stop, force-stop and cleanup retry

sequenceDiagram participant U as Stop caller participant P as Portal stop owner participant C as Generation coordinator participant S as Host supervisor participant W as Owned processes U->>P: Stop instance P->>P: Share shielded stop task and mark desired stopped P->>C: Cancel and join coordinator cleanup opt Concurrent force-stop U->>P: Escalate existing stop P->>S: Force termination before waiting for coordinator join S->>W: Signal owned groups, descendants and cgroup end P->>S: Stop generation on every member S->>W: Drain output, terminate and escalate if needed alt Cleanup verified S->>S: Remove children, leases and placement records P->>S: Re-read workers and reservation P->>P: Clear endpoint and metrics, publish stopped else Cleanup incomplete S->>S: Retain ownership and reservation P->>P: Publish failure and retain cleanup identity P-->>U: Retry Stop after resolving the failure end

Ordinary cleanup switches log readers to unconditional drains so blocked output cannot prevent exit. It sends termination, allows a ten-second grace period and then uses kill with a five-second wait. Owned descendants are also checked; zombie entries do not count as surviving work. Discovery retains known descendants, and after a leader exits it inspects the original process group/session only if the leader PID is no longer present. Cgroup cleanup verifies emptiness when available.

Force-stop signals before waiting for the cleanup lock. A retained force flag also catches children registered by a launch that already held that lock. Both normal and force callers join the same cleanup owner; caller cancellation does not abandon it. Stale generation requests are rejected. Any incomplete child/cgroup cleanup retains ownership and reservations for an explicit retry. Portal then verifies every member reports neither workers nor reservation before publishing stopped.

Worker maintenance checks expired leases every five seconds and retries failed cleanup on later passes. Stopping one fitting trial is narrower: it checks generation and engine PID, removes that engine after cleanup and retains the generation's GPU/port/RAM reservation for subsequent trials.

Service lifetime and restart intent

sequenceDiagram participant A as Standalone service control participant P as Portal participant S as Supervisor and store participant X as Process exit owner A->>A: Reject conflicting action or active management writes A->>P: Drain with restart intent when requested P->>P: Stop scans and reject new instances/jobs P->>S: Stop instances, cancel jobs and reap orphan-owned workers opt Restart was requested P->>S: Restore saved running intent even after failure end alt Cleanup fails P->>P: Reopen management for recovery A-->>A: Retain failure without calling exit owner else Cleanup succeeds A->>X: Invoke supplied exit handler end Note over A,X: The Controller uses its own subsystem lifecycle instead

Standalone service control owns one cleanup task and invokes its supplied exit handler only after drain succeeds. The standalone API tracks active management writes and fences new writes while draining. Repeated identical service actions share the task; a conflicting action is rejected. Startup without an exit handler does not expose a working service-exit command.

Drain captures desired-running instances that still have saved profiles. Restart restores their intent in a finally block, including after failed cleanup; shutdown leaves stopped intent. Orphan workers/jobs are also reconciled. Startup creates fresh process ownership, clears old reservation records, marks formerly active jobs interrupted and can schedule desired-running instances from successful requests. Clearing stale records alone is not proof that an old OS process exited. Controller integration disables automatic Portal restoration and owns its separate recovery ordering.

Portal JSON records commit through its SQLite/WAL store, with optional revision increments in Controller mode. Process handles and coordinating tasks are live memory ownership; successful snapshots are persisted recovery inputs. Secrets use a separate private replacement file and are not encrypted by this store. These are distinct from the Controller's core RAM domains and checkpoint publication.

Evidence and limits

Shutdown tests exercise owned temporary processes, port release, blocked readers, descendant cleanup, disconnected callers, force-stop races and retained ownership. Selected service-drain tests check restart intent and failed cleanup without exiting the running development service. Planner tests, cluster tests, rank-readiness tests, recommendation tests and selected RAM reservation tests use synthetic inventories and substituted backend calls.

These checks establish the exercised control flow, not actual GPU fit, network performance, distributed backend compatibility or successful native inference. Tensor search, installers/download workers and diagnostic internals retain their separate source owners; this page shows where launch invokes them.
